text:
I rowed out to my fishing ground. The weather had turned oppressive, the mosquitoes gathered in swarms, and I had to smoke tobacco the whole time to save myself. The haddock were biting; I hauled in the two-hook line; I made a good catch. On the way home I shot two auks.

When I reached the pier, the smith was standing there. He was at work. A thought passes through me, and I ask him:

May I go home with you?
No, he answers, Mr. Mack has given me work until midnight.

I nodded and thought to myself that this was good.

I took my catch with me and went, taking the road past the smith’s house. Eva was home alone.

I have longed for you so dearly, I said to her. And I was moved at the sight of her; she could scarcely look at me for astonishment. I love your youth and your good eyes, I said. Punish me today because I have thought more of another than of you. Listen, I come to you only to look at you; you do me good, I am in love with you. Did you hear me calling for you last night?

No, she answered in alarm.

I called for Edvarda, Miss Edvarda, but I meant you. It woke me. Yes, I meant you; I was excused—I misspoke when I said Edvarda. But let us speak no more of her. God, how you are my dearest girl, Eva! Your mouth is so red today. You have prettier feet than Edvarda; just look for yourself. — I lifted her dress and showed her her own legs.

A joy I had never yet seen in her flew across her face; she is about to turn away, but thinks better of it and puts one arm around my neck.

Some time passes. We talk together, sit all the while on a long bench, and talk to each other about many things. I said:

Would you believe it, Miss Edvarda has not yet learned to speak; she talks like a child, she says “more happier”; I have heard it myself. Do you think she has a beautiful forehead? I do not. She has a devilish forehead. Nor does she wash her hands.

Were we not supposed to speak no more of her?

Quite right. I merely forgot.

Some time passes again. I am thinking of something; I am silent.

Why are your eyes growing wet? Eva asks.

She has a beautiful forehead, by the way, I say, and her hands are always clean. It was only by chance that they were dirty once. I did not mean to say otherwise. — But now I continue heatedly and through clenched teeth: I sit constantly thinking of you, Eva; but it occurs to me that perhaps you have not heard what I am about to tell you. The first time Edvarda saw Aesop, she said: Aesop, why, he was a wise man; he was a Phrygian. Is that not ridiculous? She had read it in a book that same day, I am certain of it.

Yes, says Eva, but what of it?

As far as I remember, she also spoke of Aesop having had Xanthus as his teacher. Hahaha.

I see.
What the devil is the point of telling a gathering that Aesop had Xanthus as his teacher? I am merely asking. Ah, you are not in the mood today, Eva, otherwise you would laugh yourself sick over it.

Yes, I think it is amusing too, says Eva, and begins to laugh with effort and astonishment. But I do not understand it as well as you do.

I am silent and think, silent and thinking.

Would you rather that we sit quietly and say nothing? Eva asks softly. Goodness shone from her eyes; she stroked my hair with her hand.

You good, good soul! I exclaim, pressing her fiercely to me. I am certain I shall perish from love for you; I love you more and more; in the end you will come with me when I leave. You will see. Could you come with me?

Yes, she answers.

I scarcely hear this yes, but I feel it in her breath, I sense it in her; we hold each other wildly, and she gives herself to me so senselessly.

An hour later I kiss Eva farewell and leave. I meet Mr. Mack in the doorway.

Mr. Mack himself.

He starts and stares into the room, remains standing there on the threshold and staring. Well! he says, and cannot manage to say more; he is as though struck senseless.

You had not expected to find me here? I say, greeting him.

Eva does not move.

Mr. Mack collects himself; a remarkable assurance settles over him, and he answers:

You are mistaken; it is precisely you I am looking for. I wish to make you aware that from the first of April until the fifteenth of August, it is forbidden to fire shots within one eighth of a mile of an egg-and-down nesting ground. Today you shot two birds by the island; there are people who saw you.

I shot two auks, I said, stricken. It dawned on me on the spot that the man was within his rights.

Two auks or two eider ducks, it is all the same. You were within the protected area.

I acknowledge it, I said. It had not occurred to me until now.

But it ought to have occurred to you before now.

I also fired both barrels in roughly the same place in the month of May. It was on an island excursion. It happened at your own request.

That is another matter, Mr. Mack said curtly.
But then, for the devil’s sake, you surely know what you have to do?

Very well indeed, he answered.

Eva had held herself in readiness; when I went out, she followed, having put on a kerchief, and walked away from the house; I saw her take the road down to the piers. Mr. Mack walked home.

I thought it over. What agility in contriving a way out—how his eyes stabbed! One shot, two shots, a couple of auks, a fine, a payment. And then everything, everything was settled with Mr. Mack and his house. Fundamentally, it all went so exceedingly smoothly and quickly....

It had already begun to rain in large, soft drops. The magpies flew close to the ground, and when I came home and let Aesop loose, it ate grass. The wind began to sigh.

XXIII

A mile below me I see the sea. It is raining, and I am up in the mountains; a rock overhang shelters me from the rain. I smoke my short pipe, smoke one pipe after another, and each time I light it, the tobacco crawls upward like tiny glowing worms out of the ash. Thus, too, the thoughts swarm in my head. Before me on the ground lies a bundle of dry twigs from a ruined bird’s nest. And as this bird’s nest is, so too is my soul.

I remember every smallest trifle of the experiences of this day and the next. Hoho, how badly I was mauled....

I sit here up in the mountains, and the sea and the air roar; wind and weather seethe and lament horribly in my ears. Freighters and yachts can be seen far out with reefed sails; there are people aboard, they must be going somewhere, and God knows where all these lives are going, I think. The sea rises foaming into the air and tumbles, tumbles; it is as though peopled by great, raging figures that fling out their limbs and roar at one another—no, it is a revel among ten thousand shrieking devils who duck their heads between their shoulders and wheel around, whipping the sea white with the tips of their wings. Far, far out lies a submerged reef; from this reef a white merman rises and shakes his head after a leaking square-rigger running before the wind out to sea—hoho, out to sea, out into the desolate sea....
